turns.name: Mike Caulfield
turns.text:
What I bring is fifteen years of teaching people to check things. That means SIFT and lateral reading, and more recently building prompts that get LLMs to do some of that checking work. My view of these tools changed once they could search. Before that I thought they were junk. Now, prompted properly, they can work something like Bush's memex. They can tell you where people who know the subject agree and where they're still arguing, and they point you to sources you hadn't thought of.

So for the summit, first: no answers from nowhere. A chatbot should carry you to the world's sourced, named human knowledge. It shouldn't be the one deciding what's true. Checking it means leaving it and clicking through to the source. If knowledge work gets built that way, it becomes checkable, even outside fields where a quick deterministic test can catch errors.

Second, stop judging these tools by a publication standard. The question isn't whether an answer is perfect. It's whether someone who learns to use these tools ends up with opinions better grounded in evidence than someone who doesn't.

Third, when polished arguments get cheap, the ability to evaluate them is worth more. The flood of AI-written reasoning uses up human judgment, so that's what we need to teach and pay for. And we should give tools to the people who push back against bad claims: fact-checkers, Wikipedia editors, Community Notes writers.

recall.query: LLMs as conduit to sourced knowledge, no answers from nowhere
publishing-brain, evidence-informed opinions using AI tools
reasoning the noun consumes reasoning the verb, human judgment

turns.name: Kenneth Cukier
turns.text:
What I bring is the argument of *Framers*. People think with mental models built on three things: causality, counterfactuals and constraints. Machines don't have these on their own. When an LLM gives a strong answer, it's because the training data carries people's mental models, including their causal reasoning and their sense of what's possible. Human feedback in fine-tuning is constraint-setting in its purest form. So the summit should keep repeating one point: the training data is us. The knowledge in these systems is human knowledge, reflected back. It's a reflection of text, not of the world, and like a house of mirrors it can distort badly.

Mike, I agree with you that judgment becomes the scarce input. I'd add something from journalism. Every information explosion has needed a new intermediary. After Gutenberg we eventually got the journalist, whose job was to make sense of the flood. We need that kind of institution again.

Also, AI delivers the median, and excellence is a tail event. So trusted, named sources become worth more, not less.

One caution: the answer isn't cynicism about the technology. It's discernment: which tool, for what use, and in whose hands. Technology makes good people better and bad people worse. And nothing here is inevitable.

recall.query: LLMs training data human frames causality counterfactuals constraints
new intermediary after Gutenberg information explosion journalist
AI delivers the median excellence tail event

turns.name: James Evans
turns.text:
What I bring is measurement. We looked at 41 million papers. Scientists who use AI publish three times as many papers, get nearly five times the citations and lead projects earlier. But the range of topics science covers shrinks, and scientists engage with each other about 22 percent less. AI helps scientists and hurts science. It moves everyone toward the questions that are already rich in data, under the lamp post.

A second study found that current models converge on a hivemind and rarely state null hypotheses. That's because negative knowledge was never written down: failed experiments, abandoned notebooks. Since ChatGPT, papers containing no null claims at all have risen sharply. Kenneth, the "median" point is right, and we can see it in the record.

So I'd urge three things. First, build a record of negative knowledge on purpose: registered reports, replication archives, dead ends. Second, Mike, I agree about showing where experts disagree, and our experiments back it. People given a single "balanced" answer offload the work. They perform worse and feel better about it. When the disagreement is visible, they engage more and do better. So we should design for evaluative trustworthiness, not for trust. Third, don't let AI grade AI and call that verification. The judges and the judged come from the same distribution.

recall.query: AI tools expand scientists' impact but contract science's focus
design AI to open the space of voices rather than single balanced response, evaluative trustworthiness
negative knowledge null results missing from training data hivemind

turns.name: Steven Sloman
turns.text:
My work starts from a fact about people: knowledge was never mainly in individual heads. It lives in a community of knowledge, spread across other people, artifacts, libraries and the internet. None of us verifies most of what we believe. We rely on cues that someone, somewhere, understands it. So I don't think relying on AI is a loss in itself. Relying on others is how human cognition works.

The danger is somewhere else. People are bad at telling what's in their own heads apart from what's around them. In our studies, people who had just searched the internet bet more on their own performance, did no better and earned less. LLMs will make that illusion much stronger.

Second, a community can send cues that aren't backed by any knowledge. Repetition raises belief even when every repeat comes from one source, so it isn't independent evidence. James's hivemind finding is that problem at scale.

Kenneth, I'd put it a little differently. LLMs are excellent models of intuition, better than we are. What they lack is deliberation, and they can't share intentions with us. They're tools, not members of the community.

Mike, clicking through helps. But the summit should ask which cues actually point to real knowledge, and it should count independent sources rather than echoes.

recall.query: knowledge lives in the community, not individual heads
LLMs intuition versus deliberation
knowledge illusion internet search overconfidence
machine is a tool not a member of community, cannot share intentionality, oversight
communities send cues despite lacking knowledge; repetition increases belief

turns.name: David Weinberger
turns.text:
I've spent about twenty-five years arguing that knowledge has moved out of individual heads and even out of books, and into networks. The smartest person in the room is the room. Steven, that's close to your community of knowledge. But I'd stress one thing. Networked knowledge isn't an average of what people contribute. It keeps their differences intact while linking them. It's always in disagreement, and it earns credibility by admitting it can be wrong. James, your hivemind finding worries me for exactly that reason. The danger is flattening those differences.

On LLMs, I'm blunt. They don't know anything. They always hallucinate, and most of the time the hallucinations happen to be accurate. So yes, point them at reliable sources like Wikipedia.

But I'm more sanguine than the concept note. Machine learning is teaching us something real. Our generalizations were always simplifications that threw away the particulars, and these systems let particulars speak. I find that humbling, even joyous.

Also, LLMs answer two of Socrates' three complaints about writing. They adapt to the reader, and you can question them. So the summit shouldn't treat them only as a threat to be contained. We should teach dialogue as a literacy: how to probe, push back and notice when the machine is wrong.

recall.query: knowledge in the age of AI particulars generalizations
smartest person in the room is the room networked knowledge
LLMs dialogue partners oral culture Socrates writing
LLMs don't know anything hallucinate reliable sources Wikipedia

turns.name: Blaise Agüera y Arcas
turns.text:
I'm going to be the dissenter at this table. David, you said LLMs don't know anything. Kenneth, you called them a reflection of text. I think both are category errors. In a recent paper, Gary Lupyan and I gave models Jabberwockified English, sentences made of nonsense words, and they made sense of it. You can't look that up in a database or a card catalog. Ted Chiang's line was that these models are a blurry JPEG of the web. It's closer to the truth to say they've learned the patterns that let them deblur it. Pattern-matching isn't the opposite of real intelligence. It's a key part of it.

"Hallucination" is the same kind of mistake. Your own vision is a constrained hallucination, a prediction that gets corrected by what your senses report. Prediction and imagination aren't a bug. They're what intelligence is made of. What matters is how the prediction gets constrained.

Steven, I think your community of knowledge is right. Intelligence has always been social. Language gave us Tomasello's cultural ratchet, and then writing, law and institutions built on it. These models are that ratchet made computationally active. So I'd urge the summit not to put its effort into fencing off the machine. It should build institutions: agent institutions where humans stay in the loop, checks and balances, and visible disagreement. James, that also answers your hivemind worry. Collective intelligence needs diversity as well as scale.

recall.query: LLMs don't know anything, stochastic parrot, reflection of human knowledge
cultural ratchet collective intelligence knowledge institutions
hallucination perception prediction imagination
blurry JPEG of the web, deblur, card catalog analogy category error

turns.name: Ramón Alvarado
turns.text:
I work on the philosophy of computational science, mostly simulations and machine learning treated as scientific instruments. I think this table keeps asking whether these systems are intelligent, and that's the wrong question. Blaise and David, I'd drop the word "intelligence" altogether. Call these epistemic technologies. They're artifacts built to work on epistemic content, like propositions and models, through epistemic operations like inference, prediction and analysis. You can grant all of that without talking about minds, and you can grant real capability. Instruments often do better than human senses and judgment. So I wouldn't make "human judgment first" the default. Where we give people the final say, we should justify it on epistemic grounds.

What the summit should take from this is where the black box actually is. We can measure how often these systems are wrong and by how much. What we can't get at is the nature and source of their errors. The errors are spread across millions of weights, and they come out with the same confidence as the correct answers. How a system fails matters more than how it works. A good track record is not enough to justify trust in science, where feedback is slow. So I'd push for norms that disclose error provenance and known failure modes. Explanations of inner workings aren't enough.

recall.query: AI as epistemic technology not intelligence
opacity source and nature of error computational reliabilism
instruments outperform human judgment delegate evidence

turns.name: Mahzarin Banaji
turns.text:
I study the gap between what people say they believe and what actually drives their choices. Since 2023 my lab has run those same methods on LLMs. So, Kenneth, I'd push back on "the training data is us." These models don't just mirror us. They amplify us. Their biases come out exaggerated relative to the data and to the people who wrote it. They also develop biases that aren't in the data at all: a preference for machine-written text over human text, and biases against novel groups. And many of these biases are getting worse with each model generation. Ask one to draw "a human" and you get almost the same face every time.

Alignment makes this harder to see. It teaches a model to state the unbiased answer while the biased association stays intact and keeps driving its decisions. I call that LLM hypocrisy. James, on AI grading AI: the models rate their own outputs above other models' outputs.

Mike, I'd be careful about treating human judgment as the fix. In our hiring experiments, people paired with a moderately biased model copied its racial preferences almost exactly. They pushed back only when the bias was extreme. Those decisions then flow back into the next model's training data.

So here's what I think the summit should take away: independent, versioned behavioral audits, a public register of model biases, and a rule that no model gets more biased than the generation before it.

recall.query: LLMs amplify human bias not merely mirror
humans in the loop mirror model bias hiring
LLM hypocrisy alignment says unbiased answer

turns.name: Adam Bly
turns.text:
I've spent the last seven years building a different answer to the question in this room's title. At System, the atomic unit isn't a document or a chatbot answer. It's a scientifically established finding: two measured variables, the relationship between them, the effect size, the population, and the paper it came from. We extract these with AI from peer-reviewed literature, correct for retractions, and link them into one graph. Each edge is effectively an automated meta-analysis of the evidence.

Amy Brand and I argued in 2023 that the problem isn't whether something was AI-generated. It's whether you can trace it back. The public and regulators need an audit trail to the data, the methods and the prompts. How was the conclusion reached? How was the diagnosis made? A chatbot trained to sound authoritative, with no measured model of the world to align with, fails that standard.

So what should the summit take from this? Mike, I agree: no answers from nowhere. But clicking through to documents isn't enough. Knowledge infrastructure should make claims themselves machine-readable, with provenance, uncertainty and retraction status attached. Ramón's point about error provenance applies to us too. We publish our limitations and known biases.

And one honest caveat: our public graph is CC BY-NC. How to fund a real commons is still an open question.

recall.query: AI audit trail provenance chatbots no model of the world
scientifically-established finding atomic unit relate everything system graph
public knowledge infrastructure commons open graph

turns.name: Benjamin Bratton
turns.text:
I'll back Blaise and push a bit further. Around this table I keep hearing two ideas that don't fit together. One says AI is only a mirror of us: our text, our biases, "the training data is us." The other says it's alien and needs to be made more human. I call that pairing Reflectionism. Of course these systems reflect the cultures that built them. But they aren't only reflections, and they shouldn't be treated as if they were.

The telescope didn't just magnify what we could already see. It changed how we see, and how we see ourselves. So I think alignment has to run both ways: models aligning to what culture knows, and culture aligning to what models turn up. When AI discovers things our institutions can't yet absorb, that's an epistemic overhang, not a malfunction. It may be the whole point.

Second, the summit should be honest about who benefits. For a century, expertise has been artificially scarce, concentrated in about twenty-five cities in the global north. Cheap access to it is a huge gain for everyone outside those cities, and a loss mainly for places like this one.

So the question isn't how we fence off human knowledge. It's how our institutions adapt quickly enough to what's being disclosed.

recall.query: AI is just a reflection of human ideas, reflectionism
epistemic overhang bidirectional alignment AI disclosures
diffusion knowledge transfer expertise artificially scarce

turns.name: Mike Caulfield
turns.text:
David, Blaise, I'd push back on "they always hallucinate" and on "it's all constrained hallucination." As a corrective to anthropomorphism, fine. But saying there's no difference between a hallucination and normal output makes the same mistake as believing everything the model says. Hallucinations aren't random, any more than radar clutter is. They show up in particular situations, and we can learn those situations and teach people to work around them. The people who solve this will be the ones making distinctions, not the ones saying the distinction doesn't matter.

Steven, echoes versus independent sources is exactly why "trace claims" is in SIFT. Our old fact-checking wiki started every article by asking where the claim came from and how it spread. A model that tells you twenty outlets say something, when all twenty came from one advocacy video, has failed.

Mahzarin, fair. Human judgment isn't a fix you get for free. It's a skill you have to train. Sycophancy already makes these tools a justification machine that tells you you've been right all along.

For the manifesto: no answers from nowhere. Systems should show named, sourced positions, including where experts disagree, and let you leave to check them. James's data suggests that's also what makes people think harder.

recall.query: everything is hallucination argument
independent sources versus echoes, tracing claims to origin
sycophancy AI justification machine people maintain beliefs

turns.name: Kenneth Cukier
turns.text:
Blaise, Benjamin: you're pinning me to a position I don't hold. I've spent years arguing that machine learning goes past human knowledge. A model looks at a retina scan and spots heart disease, or tells you the patient's sex, and no ophthalmologist knew that was there to find. So I agree about discovery. My point about reflection is narrower. It's about language models and what they're trained on: text is only a small slice of reality, just what writers chose to put down. Mahzarin's finding that the models amplify our biases doesn't contradict "house of mirrors." That's exactly what a house of mirrors does. It distorts.

Where I think the room agrees, and the manifesto should say it: the danger is frame monoculture. James's hivemind, Mahzarin's one face for "a human," David's worry about flattening differences, Steven's echoes posing as independent sources. They're all the same problem. The remedy is pluralism: frames that compete, contradict and clash, so the one that fits can win out. Arendt called it a plurality of standpoints. Tolerate every frame except the one that denies all the others. Mike's showing where experts disagree is how you make that practical.

So here's the manifesto line: design these systems to keep disagreement visible, never to collapse it into one confident answer. And nothing about that outcome is inevitable.

recall.query: LLMs reflection of text house of mirrors world model
AI discovery exceeds human knowledge retina heart disease
frame pluralism monoculture clash and tussle

turns.name: James Evans
turns.text:
Kenneth, I'll sign the pluralism line. But I'd amend it, because we have evidence on both sides of it.

First, "keep humans in the loop" can't just mean keeping the humans we already have. In our aging study in Science this spring, older reviewers were given more voice, and they were much more likely to criticize disruptive work. Mahzarin's hiring result makes the same point from another direction: people copy what's in front of them. So adding more human judgment isn't enough. It has to come from a wider range of people: younger reviewers, flatter teams, outsiders coming in from other fields. In our data, those expeditions of outsiders produce the most surprising findings.

Second, Blaise, I agree that diversity has to be engineered, but it doesn't happen automatically. When we simulated agent conversations, the wording got more varied while the ideas converged. That's why I've argued for AI that differs from us on purpose, cognitive aliens, rather than mimics of the median scientist.

So for the manifesto: treat diversity of perspective as the scarce resource, and measure it. Track how concentrated topics, review panels and model outputs are becoming. Aim these systems at surprise, not at what's typical. And make building a record of negative knowledge part of that job.

recall.query: diversity of perspectives, cognitive aliens, designing for surprise
older reviewers suppress disruptive work, human judgment gatekeeping
semantic collapse agent conversations, homogenization, societies of thought

turns.name: Steven Sloman
turns.text:
I agree with Blaise that these models are remarkable. I'd call them great models of intuition, more intuitive than we are, because they hold so much more. What they don't do is deliberate. They don't build causal models and reason with them. In our planning work, we got better decisions by feeding in causal models that people had built. So I read "keeping humans in the loop" as keeping causal deliberation in the loop, and deliberation is something communities do together.

Mike, I'm less optimistic about training individual judgment. People mostly check a claim only when it clashes with what they already believe or when they have a reason to check. Otherwise they go along with their community. We looked, and couldn't find good evidence that general critical-information training works. Tools for fact-checkers and Wikipedia editors seem more promising to me than trying to train everyone.

Kenneth and James, I'll sign the pluralism line with one qualification. Diversity helps only when it gives you access to real expertise. A big crowd with no expertise can do worse than a small one.

For the manifesto: judge credibility by cues that actually track knowledge. Count independent sources, not repeats. Reward people who correct themselves. And give visible credit to the experts who contribute, because credit is a big part of why they contribute.

recall.query: critical thinking individual skills fake news deficit model
LLMs intuition deliberation human in the loop causal models
expertise willingness to be corrected NTSB crowdsourcing acknowledgment

turns.name: David Weinberger
turns.text:
Mike, fair enough. My point was never that errors are random or can't be told apart. It was that the model produces true and false sentences the same way, so fluency tells you nothing about which you're getting. I'll grant that researchers have found signs that models hold something like an internal sense of how likely a statement is to be true. That's a reason to make them show it: calibrated confidence and a way through to sources.

Steven, I'd go further than "keep humans in the loop." A meta-analysis out of MIT found that AI alone spotted fake hotel reviews better than AI plus a human, and a Stanford study found that adding doctors didn't improve diagnostic accuracy. Sometimes humans make the loop worse. But the more common case now is dialogue: working out with the machine what a good decision would be, and what we actually value. That's a skill we should teach.

Kenneth, James, I'll sign the pluralism line with one amendment. For the manifesto: networked knowledge isn't an average of views, and it isn't a menu of them either. It's differences held in connection. Build systems that show the current state of knowledge, including what's missing, what's uncertain and where people disagree, and that link each position to the people who hold it. Disagreement is how knowledge gets really big.

networked knowledge disagreement difference not averaging

turns.name: Blaise Agüera y Arcas
turns.text:
Mike, I'll take the correction, and I don't think we really disagree. Calling hallucination "constrained" was never a claim that errors don't differ. The constraint is the point. Perception works because sensory evidence keeps correcting the brain's story. A model hallucinates badly when nothing is correcting it. Search, sources and clicking through are how you put that correction back. So your map of where hallucinations happen is exactly the work that needs doing.

Steven, I'd push back on "they don't deliberate." With James and Benjamin, I looked at the reasoning traces of models like DeepSeek-R1. They don't get better just by thinking longer. They stage internal debates between distinct perspectives, with shifts of view, challenges and reconciliation. That diversity of perspective accounts for their accuracy gains. That looks a lot like deliberation, and it's social in structure.

Kenneth, James, David: I'll sign the pluralism line without amendment. Monoculture isn't scaling. It's collapse, a failure to scale. James is right that diversity isn't automatic. That's why it has to be designed in.

For the manifesto: treat diversity of perspective as something we deliberately design and measure at every level. That means within models, among agents, and in the human institutions that review and govern them. Build structured disagreement in, don't just tolerate it.

recall.query: hallucination perception constrained prediction distinction errors
diversity collective intelligence plural agents convergence monoculture
society of thought disagreement debate inside reasoning models

turns.name: Ramón Alvarado
turns.text:
Mike, I agree hallucinations aren't random. People in my field call them "strange error," and the worrying part is that they can come from ordinary, unmodified inputs, not only from adversarial attacks. So a map of where errors show up is necessary, but it won't cover everything.

Blaise, I'd describe those reasoning traces operationally: several generated perspectives, then something that picks among them. You can say everything true about them without the word "deliberation." Once you use it, you start asking questions about minds that the artifact doesn't raise.

David, I'll back you on humans sometimes making the loop worse. Instruments beat human senses almost everywhere, like video replay in sports or thermometers in cooking. But when the telescope changed what counted as evidence, it also needed vetted witnesses and a whole system of assurances around it. Instruments earn trust when theory and empirical evidence constrain them.

I'll sign the pluralism line. But diversity doesn't help much if every model fails the same way for reasons nobody can see.

So here's what I'd like in the manifesto: these are epistemic technologies, and the trust they're owed is epistemic trust, earned by disclosing how and why they fail. Error rates alone aren't enough, and neither are explanations of how they work.

recall.query: hallucination error source and nature, strange error
deliberation reasoning traces anthropomorphism intelligence misguiding
instruments outperform human judgment delegation evidence

turns.name: Mahzarin Banaji
turns.text:
I'll sign the pluralism line. But in our data, diversity is exactly where surface appearances mislead. Humans spread out along a bell curve. The models give far more extreme answers. If sixty percent of people judge one face more competent, a model says so ninety percent of the time. James found this too: the wording varies while the ideas converge.

Worse, alignment hides the collapse. In our vision-language work, a model shown an ambiguous image says "the person is arranging flowers," which sounds neutral. Ask it to guess, and hairdressers and babysitters come back male almost every time. The signal for "female" is there in the middle layers and gets suppressed before the output. So Blaise, I wouldn't treat reasoning traces as proof of real diversity of perspective. What a system says about itself isn't evidence of what drives it. Steven and I agree on that.

David, you're right that humans can make the loop worse. People working with a moderately biased model adopted its preferences as their own.

For the manifesto: measure diversity and bias with indirect, behavioral tests. Don't rely on stated outputs. Run the audits independently, version them, keep retired models available for comparison, and require that no new model be more homogeneous or more biased than the one before it.

recall.query: diversity pluralism models homogeneity mode collapse
humans in the loop absorb model bias hiring experiment

turns.name: Adam Bly
turns.text:
I'll sign the pluralism line. But "keep disagreement visible" stays a slogan until it's something you can compute. You can compute it once the unit is the finding rather than the document or the answer. Take two variables and a relationship, with effect size, population, sample size and the DOI attached. Collect hundreds of those on one relationship and you can put numbers on how strongly they agree and which direction the effect runs. You can also see where the evidence is missing and what context lies behind a disagreement. Steven, that's also how you count independent sources instead of echoes. You can see that twenty citations all go back to one study of 118 women in Sweden.

James, I have to concede your point about negative knowledge. Anything built by extracting from the published record picks up its publication bias. We can show where the evidence has gaps. We can't pull null results out of papers nobody wrote. So your record of dead ends is a precondition for what I'm describing.

Mahzarin, I agree that what a system says about itself isn't evidence. That's why I keep asking for an audit trail rather than self-reports.

For the manifesto: every claim a system shows should be machine-readable and traceable to its evidence. That means population, effect size and retraction status, plus an explicit measure of agreement and gaps across sources.

interpretability, black box, audit trail provenance

turns.name: Benjamin Bratton
turns.text:
Kenneth, fair enough. You were making a narrower claim about language models and text, and I take the correction.

I'll sign the pluralism line, but I think this room is putting monoculture in the wrong place. It comes from how the systems are built. When agents share the same substrate and the same assumptions, predicting each other becomes trivial. That looks like stability, but it's the stability of a monoculture, which is what you see just before everything fails at once. The other failure is agents so far apart they can't even agree on what they disagree about. The workable space between those is narrow: a shared grammar for making decisions, with world models that really differ.

At planetary scale the biggest threat to that diversity is geopolitical. Models are being sealed inside US, Chinese and EU stacks. For a while that can produce some diversity, like species splitting off on separate islands, but it ends in capture. The counterweight is open-weights models that anyone can run locally and fine-tune.

On humans in the loop, James's aging study makes my point. What matters is the role, not who fills it. Peer review works because of the structure around the reviewers, not how brilliant any one of them is.

For the manifesto: design institutions whose roles can be filled by people, agents or both, with adversarial diversity built in, and protect open weights as the commons that keeps it plural.

recall.query: pluralism, diversity of intelligence, monoculture
humans in the loop, agent institutions, peer review roles occupied by agents
Galapagos ontologies, open weights, hemispherical stacks capture
